tasks.extracted: Table 1 (p. 2224), alcohol-attributable deaths in 2004 in thousands, against a counterfactual of no alcohol consumption, numbers rounded to the nearest thousand and printed without uncertainty intervals: cancer 377 in men (18.5% of the deaths alcohol caused in men) and 111 in women (25.0%), 487 in total; all deaths caused 2039 in men, 443 in women, 2482 in total. Cancers counted (p. 2226): mouth and oropharynx, oesophagus, colon and rectum, liver, breast and other neoplasms, colorectal cancer having been added after the 2007 assessment of the International Agency for Research on Cancer.

tasks.locator: Results › Characteristics of the included studies, 1st paragraph; Table 1
tasks.extracted: 17 studies, 9 from the USA, 4 from Italy, 2 from Denmark and one each from China and Japan, published 1980 to 2003 (Table 1), gave 12 datasets for women and 15 for men, with 1,477,887 people and 3384 cases of liver cirrhosis; seven reported women and men separately, two women only, five men only and three both sexes combined. The largest are American cohorts: Garfinkel et al. 1988 (548 185 women), Thun et al. 1997 (457 423 people) and Boffetta and Garfinkel 1990 (239 462 men), as printed in Table 1. Editors' comparison with the newer review's study list: Garfinkel 1988, Boffetta and Garfinkel 1990, Fuchs 1995, Klatsky 2003 and the Corrao case–control studies of 1993 and 1997 are in both.

tasks.locator: Results › Dose–response meta-analyses and potential threshold effects, 3rd and 5th paragraphs (p. 441); Table 2 (p. 442)
tasks.extracted: Women had higher relative risks than men for the same amount in both mortality and morbidity studies, each against lifetime abstainers of the same sex: for five drinks a day in mortality studies 14.7 (95% CI 11.0–19.6) in women and 7.0 (5.8–8.5) in men, the difference being smaller in morbidity studies (Table 2, >48–60 g: 5.9, 3.7–9.3, against 2.3, 1.7–3.2; >36–48 g: 1.9, 1.4–2.6, against 2.0, 1.5–2.7). Continuous model, women: mortality 4.9 (4.0–6.2) at 24 g and 12.5 (8.8–17.7) at 60 g a day, morbidity 3.2 (2.6–3.9) and 6.2 (4.4–8.7); men showed a similar but less pronounced pattern, shown only as curves. No test of the sex difference is reported.

Alcoholic cirrhosis developed in 257 men and 85 women, an incidence of 66 per 100,000 person-years in men and 19 in women. Median weekly amount at baseline, in drinks of 12 g, among people drinking daily: men 26 (5th–95th percentile 9.4–60), women 19 (7.3–40); among people drinking two to four days a week: men 8.9 (3.6–13), women 6.6 (3.0–19).

tasks.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Strengths and limitations, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Among women the authors say they cannot draw firm conclusions because of low statistical power; only 35% of those invited took part; women's incidence was somewhat lower than expected from national data; women in particular may be reluctant to report drinking; the low number of cases among women is a limitation.

tasks.locator: Introduction, last paragraph; Materials and methods › Study population; Information on alcohol consumption; Statistical analysis, 1st and 6th paragraphs; Results, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Danish Diet, Cancer and Health cohort: Danish-born men and women aged 50 to 64 invited from December 1993 to May 1997; 55,917 participants analysed. Weekly amounts of beer (330 ml bottles), wine (125 ml glasses) and liquor (30 ml drinks) converted to standard drinks of 12 g of ethanol; drinking frequency in seven categories from never to daily; recalled amounts at ages 20–29, 30–39, 40–49 and 50–59; all from one baseline questionnaire. Cox models with age as the time axis, adjusted for smoking (never, former, under or over 10 g of tobacco a day), education and waist circumference, all stratified by sex. Only average amount and frequency were recorded, so binge drinking could not be explored.
